--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.lattice_reference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Build a lattice-like reference graph with the same degrees. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.lattice_reference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Build a lattice-like reference graph with the same degrees. title: >- [Graph.lattice_reference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Build a lattice-like reference graph with the same degrees. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Build a lattice-like reference graph with the same degrees. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L36912-L37000){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.lattice_reference( iterations=5, connectivity=True, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Lattice reference graph](../assets/graphs/lattice-reference.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a randomly wired eight-node graph with average clustering 0.229. Right: lattice_reference(seed=1) keeps every degree but only accepts swaps that shorten edges around the ring A to H: the four long accent edges on the left become the four short accent edges on the right, closing four triangles around the ring, and the average clustering rises to 0.667." width="100%"} Like `random_reference()`, this rewires the graph with degree-preserving double edge swaps, but only accepts swaps that make the edges shorter on a ring of the nodes (nodes placed on a circle in ID order). The result approaches a ring lattice with the original degree sequence: highly clustered, with long paths. It is the "ordered" baseline of `small_world_omega()`. The graph is treated as undirected and simple. With `connectivity=True`, swaps that would disconnect the graph are undone. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[5]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Rewiring rounds, each attempting one swap per edge (default 5). [connectivity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), keep the graph connected. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducible results. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected, unweighted graph with the same nodes and rewired edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or has fewer than four nodes or two edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Sporns and Zwi (2004) latticize by accepting a swap of `a-b, c-d` into `a-d, c-b` only when the ring distances satisfy $d(a, d) + d(c, b) \le d(a, b) + d(c, d)$. NetworkX's `lattice_reference` instead compares $d(a, c) + d(b, d)$, which does not measure the new edges; EdgeCase uses the intended criterion, so its references are more lattice-like. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~random_reference`) : A random graph with the same degrees. [](`~small_world_omega`) : Compare a graph with random and lattice references. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A fully rewired ring has little clustering. Its lattice reference puts the edges back around the ring, and the clustering rises to that of a ring lattice: ::: {#68ed6764 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=24, k=4, p=1.0, seed=1) lattice = graph.lattice_reference(iterations=20, seed=1) ( round(graph.average_clustering_coefficient(), 3), round(lattice.average_clustering_coefficient(), 3), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.188, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: The ring is the order of the node IDs, as `layout_circular(order="id")` places them. The random graph (left) has edges across the circle; in the lattice reference (right), nearly every edge joins two nodes close together on the ring: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#a551042e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.layout_circular(order="id").plot(layout="pos", width=320, height=320) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#0cf595f6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} lattice.layout_circular(order="id").plot(layout="pos", width=320, height=320) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: The more `iterations=`, the closer the result comes to a lattice. It is the ordered baseline of `small_world_omega()`, as `random_reference()` is the random one.
